bullets: Clarke often writes about **family, the female experience, nature and Welsh identity**.
Catrin is a Welsh name, which roots the poem in Clarke’s cultural identity.
1970s: women’s experiences such as childbirth were rarely the subject of ‘serious’ poetry. Clarke places a mother’s physical, emotional experience at the centre.
The universal theme (parent and growing child) makes it relatable for any reader.

callouts.p: The guide uses descriptions, not the poem’s text. Choose three short quotations from your anthology (the rope of love, the fight, the request at the end) and learn them for when Catrin is your second poem.

core.p: Gillian Clarke (born 1937) is a Welsh poet, **National Poet of Wales** from 2008 to 2016. Catrin is the name of her own daughter; the poem appeared in her collection The Sundial (1978).

bullets: **Conflict type**: emotional, domestic conflict within a loving family; conflict between protection and freedom.
**Big message**: love and conflict are inseparable; a parent’s bond means a constant tug-of-war as the child grows independent.
**Perspective**: first-person mother addressing her daughter.
core.p: A mother recalls the birth of her daughter in a hot hospital room, describing labour as their first fight and the umbilical cord as a rope over which they struggled. In the second stanza, years later, the teenage daughter asks to go skating in the dark for another hour; the mother feels the same old rope of love and conflict pulling between them.

bullets: Two stanzas = **two time periods** that mirror each other: the past birth and the present argument.
The **rope** motif links both stanzas.
**Enjambment** creates breathless, flowing thought; caesura creates tense pauses.
The ending is **open**: no resolution.
Free verse reflects how the relationship cannot be neatly controlled.
core.p: **Free verse** in **two stanzas** (a longer first stanza for the birth, a shorter second for the present). There is no regular rhyme, and the poem reads like natural speech.

bullets: Conflict is **part of love**: birth is a ‘fight’, the cord a rope tying them together.
Conflict is **physical and emotional**.
Conflict is **cyclical and ongoing**: the traffic going round, the rope returning.
The **daughter’s independence** creates conflict with the mother’s protective instinct.
The conflict is **ordinary and universal**, unlike war poems.

callouts.p: A mother’s love for her daughter has always involved struggle, from birth to teenage independence.

bullets: The opening address remembering the child.
The hot, white hospital room and the traffic going round.
The ‘first fight’ and the rope image for the cord.
The clouded glass/tank and the words written on it.
The daughter in the present with long brown hair.
Her request to skate in the dark for one more hour.

essays.q: Compare how mothers are presented in Catrin and Poppies.
essays.text: Clarke presents motherhood as a struggle that begins with the body. The birth is described as a fight, and the umbilical cord becomes a red rope binding them in love, an image that is both a literal bond and a tug-of-war; the colour red suggests blood and love at once. Weir also presents the mother’s love through physical contact, but it is restrained and protective rather than combative: she pins a poppy on her son’s blazer and resists the urge to smooth his hair, and textile imagery suggests a mother who has spent years caring for him. Structurally, both poems move through time, but Clarke’s two stanzas mirror each other so that the past ‘fight’ and the present request are clearly linked, whereas Weir’s memories are fragmented by caesura and enjambment, as if her thoughts keep breaking off. Clarke’s ending is open and ordinary, a teenager asking to stay out longer, while Weir’s ends with the mother at a war memorial, listening for a voice she may never hear. Writing in the 1970s, Clarke made a woman’s everyday experience the subject of serious poetry; Weir, commissioned in 2009 during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, shows that the same maternal bond is tested to its limit by war.
essays.thesis: Both poets present a mother who must let go of a child, but Clarke’s mother is locked in an ongoing, loving tug-of-war with a daughter who wants freedom, while Weir’s mother has already lost her son to a war she cannot follow him into.

poem.how: In copyright: open your anthology beside this guide. Two stanzas = two moments in time.

stanzas.gist: The mother speaks directly to her child and says she can remember her: standing in a hot, white hospital room at the window, watching the traffic go round and round outside, during labour.
stanzas.label: Stanza 1, opening: the memory

notes.n: **Apostrophe/second person**: the whole poem is spoken to Catrin. Intimate, like a letter or a conversation, but also confrontational: ‘you’ is the other side in the conflict.
**Sensory imagery**: the clinical, sterile hospital is uncomfortable and impersonal. White suggests blankness or purity before the colour and passion of the birth.
**Circular imagery** of cars going round and round: the world carries on, and it foreshadows the cyclical, repeating nature of mother–daughter conflict.
Personal, **autobiographical** memory: Catrin is Clarke’s own daughter. The tone is reflective.

stanzas.gist: She describes the birth as their first fight, a struggle against each other over the red cord that joined them, which was the beginning of their separation. She says they wrote their own words on the clouded glass of the room, a sign that they each wanted something different.
stanzas.label: Stanza 1, middle–end: the ‘first fight’

notes.n: **Metaphor**: childbirth is a battle between two people who love each other. Conflict is part of love from the start.
**Extended metaphor** of the rope: a literal bond (cord) and a tug-of-war. Red = blood, passion, love and danger. Alliteration and the tight rhythm show the strain.
notes.w: The cord described as a red rope of love

notes.n: Both want to be free of each other and yet are bound: **paradox** of the parent–child bond.
The room is like a fish tank, with the mother on display. The **clouding** glass and writing on it suggest emotions too strong to see clearly through, and each trying to ‘write’ their own story.
Long, flowing sentences with **enjambment** mirror the drawn-out pain and intensity of labour.

stanzas.gist: Years later, her daughter stands in the doorway with her long brown hair, an independent child, and the old rope connects them again as she asks to be allowed to go out skating in the dark for one more hour.
stanzas.label: Stanza 2: the present-day argument

notes.n: **Volta** between stanzas: time jumps to the present. The conflict was never resolved; it continues in a new form. **Structure** mirrors two stages of the same relationship.
notes.w: The time jump between the stanzas

notes.n: **Repeated motif**: the cord has become an emotional bond, and the tug-of-war is now about freedom. The mother cannot simply cut it.
**Physical description** emphasises the child’s growth, health and independence: she is strong now, like a rope herself.
notes.w: Her straight, strong, long brown hair

notes.n: The present-day ‘conflict’ is ordinary and small (a curfew), which shows how universal parent–child tension is. ‘Dark’ hints at the mother’s fear of danger.
notes.w: Skating in the dark for one more hour

notes.n: The poem ends on the daughter’s request with **no resolution**: we never learn the mother’s answer. The conflict is ongoing, which reflects real life.

poem.title: Catrin

summary: Catrin (Gillian Clarke, published 1978) is addressed by a mother to her daughter, recalling the ‘fight’ of her birth and a present-day argument with the teenage Catrin; compare how it presents conflict within a loving relationship, the bond between parent and child, and independence, with Clarke’s Welsh and personal context.
